transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-04-02
Start: 16:00 UTC
Duration: 58 minutes
Attendees: Lena Park (Redwood AE), Diego Ramos (Redwood SE), Maya Singh (Head of ML, Cardinal HealthTech), Tom Keller (Platform Eng), Rita O'Neal (SRE), Samir Patel (CTO)

Summary: quick scoping workshop to lock down acceptance gates for the POC benchmark, agree on telemetry contract, and outline how customer scripts will integrate with Redwood's harness. Focus on streaming vs non-streaming tradeoffs for their use-pattern (short multi-turn clinical summarizations and longer document embeddings), and gating criteria for go/no-go.

Topics: success criteria, workload sizing, benchmark metrics, harness adapter, streaming vs non-streaming, KV cache warmup, telemetry payloads, timeline

Action items recap (at top): see action items metadata; will repeat at end.

Transcript body:
[00:00] Lena Park: hey everyone, thanks for making time. quick intros, uh, we'll go through acceptance gates and then dig into how you want to run your client scripts. Diego and I will capture the telemetry contract.
[00:22] Maya Singh: thanks Lena. quick context — we're trying to validate two things: first, that Redwood can hit our p95 and throughput targets on production-like traffic; second, that the cost per 1M tokens is within our budget envelope. we also have strict audit and retention needs.
[00:40] Samir Patel: and timeline, we want to decide on a vendor by end of May so the POC needs to wrap mid-May.
[01:05] Lena Park: ok, good. Diego, do you want to put the fenceposts on success criteria?
[01:12] Diego Ramos: yeah. from experience it's useful to make them concrete. suggested initial gates: p95 latency for inference under 600ms for our short-response workload (<= 128 tokens), tail cold-start 99th under 1.5s, sustained throughput of 180 req/s at 128 tokens with error rate <0.5%, and token cost target of < $6 per 1M tokens (we'll refine once we see actual quantized model numbers). also memory/kv cache warmup: 90% of requests should hit warmed KV cache after a 10 minute warm period for steady-state tests.
[01:51] Tom Keller: that lat number, 600ms p95, is for our user-facing summarization API. we do have a second workload — nightly bulk embeddings and long docs ~2k tokens — which is less sensitive to p95 but needs throughput / batch efficiency. how do we capture both in one harness?
[02:15] Diego Ramos: we'll partition the workload into slices — realtime short-turn slice and batch long-turn slice. harness can run simultaneous suites: streaming path for the realtime slice and non-streaming for batch. streaming here means chunked token streaming that reduces client-side perceived latency; non-streaming means request/response synchronous generation. the harness will replay your traces into those two lanes.
[02:42] Rita O'Neal: can you explain streaming vs non-streaming impact on our telemetry? we want consistent traces for tracing and SLO dashboards.
[02:50] Diego Ramos: yes. streaming will emit token-level partial responses and more granular timing metrics: first-byte latency, per-chunk latency, and overall finish time. non-streaming gives total response latency. we include both in the telemetry contract; we also require the client adapter to surface sequence IDs so we can correlate across retries and fallbacks.
[03:20] Maya Singh: about the client adapter — our scripts are Python-based, using a homegrown SDK. can you run their scripts directly or do we need to wrap them?
[03:30] Lena Park: two options: 1) Redwood's harness can call your scripts (we ask you to make an adapter function that takes a single test vector and returns a standardized response object), or 2) we run a traffic mirror where you send traffic to Redwood endpoints and we capture that as golden for replay. option 1 is easier for controlled benchmarking; option 2 is closer to production.
[03:55] Tom Keller: option 2 sounds attractive but we need to be careful about PHI and data residency. we can anonymize, but it might change sequences and tokenization.
[04:10] Lena Park: understood. many customers anonymize at the client side and provide a 48h scrubbed trace. that works for model perf; for cost/caching behaviors we sometimes ask for synthetic-but-representative traces that preserve length distribution and prefix patterns.
[04:32] Samir Patel: what about KV cache warmup — how much trace do you need to reach warmed state?
[04:40] Diego Ramos: for warmup we do a dedicated phase: replay a two-pass warmup where we prime prefixes and then run steady-state for 10-20 minutes. empirical rule: for many LLM workloads, the majority of cache hits happen after ~1000 distinct prefixes or after ~10 minutes of representative steady-state traffic, depends on how your prefix diversity looks. we'll instrument and report cache hit rate as part of the telemetry.
[05:12] Maya Singh: telemetry contract — can you list exact fields? we need to ensure our observability team can map them into Splunk/NewRelic.
[05:20] Diego Ramos: sure. minimal telemetry fields we'll emit: request_id, sequence_id, model_version, route (hosted|dedicated|private), deployment_zone, request_start_ts, first_byte_ts, completion_ts, token_count_input, token_count_output, kv_cache_hit (true/false), batch_size, cpu/gpu_ms (where available), error_flag, error_code, fallback_reason (if any), quantization_profile, cost_estimate_tokens. we'll provide a CSV + json schema that maps to Splunk.
[06:02] Rita O'Neal: encryption/KMS fields? we need to show where keys are used and whether payloads are stored anywhere.
[06:08] Lena Park: good point. security will add: storage_retention_flag, kms_key_id (masked), audit_log_id. we'll attach Redwood security pack.
[06:25] Tom Keller: on the harness side, we have existing runner that issues 1k rps at peak — do you need us to adapt that runner or can you accept our artifacts?
[06:36] Diego Ramos: we can accept artifacts. ideally you provide: (1) the runner invocation with parameters, (2) the script that turns a test vector into a request, and (3) a small shim adapter that converts your SDK call to the harness spec. if you can't change runner, we can mirror traffic into our harness or run sidecars that translate.
[06:57] Maya Singh: what's the recommended batch sizes? we care about both latency and cost.
[07:05] Diego Ramos: for realtime short-turn we typically use batch size 1-4 to keep latency low; for batch embeddings, larger batches (32-256) produce better throughput and token cost. the exact sweet spot depends on the model and whether quantized kernels are used. we'll run a sweep to find the knee.
[07:30] Samir Patel: will the benchmark include model variants and quantized runs? we plan to try FP16 and 8-bit quantized variants.
[07:38] Lena Park: yes, model matrix is part of the plan. Diego will coordinate which model variants we include. the harness supports fallthrough routing to cheaper variants under load, but for gating we should test the primary production variant first and then a cost-optimized variant.
[07:56] Tom Keller: what are realistic acceptance thresholds for the batch jobs? we don't expect sub-second p95 for 2k-token jobs.
[08:02] Diego Ramos: agreed. for long jobs, acceptance criteria should be: average throughput >= X tokens/sec (we'll compute based on your throughput window), error rate <1%, and median cost per document below the budgeted number. we will work with you to convert your batch SLO into numeric thresholds.
[08:28] Maya Singh: any thoughts on synthetic vs live replay tradeoffs?
[08:33] Diego Ramos: synthetic replay is faster to run and safe for PHI, but it can miss correlated user behaviors that affect caching. live replay is more accurate for cache/hot prefix behavior. we recommend a two-stage approach: synthetic first to smoke test, then a scrubbed live replay for cache-sensitive metrics.
[08:55] Samir Patel: timeline check: what does Redwood need from us to get the harness running next week?
[09:02] Lena Park: immediate asks: share the 48h scrubbed trace, one representative short-turn script, and your runner invocation. Diego will review and send the adapter spec.
[09:15] Tom Keller: ok we'll try to get that by Friday.
[09:20] \"Manual interjection, crosstalk\"
[09:28] Diego Ramos: quick note on telemetry volume — streaming emits more events; make sure Splunk ingestion is prepared or we will provide reduced sampling for token-level events.
[09:40] Rita O'Neal: sampling is fine, we need the first-byte and completion times for SLOs.
[09:46] Diego Ramos: yep. we'll sample token-level events at 1% by default and full-aggregate metrics at 100%.
[09:55] Maya Singh: acceptance window — do you do sustained runs or ramp tests?
[10:01] Diego Ramos: both. standard plan: ramp for 10 minutes to target, hold for 20-30 minutes steady-state, and a cooldown. we'll also run spike tests and durability long-run 2-3 hour tests if you want. for POC acceptance we usually do a 30-minute steady-state plus cold-start tail checks.
[10:23] Samir Patel: what about cost modeling — is that derived from actual token counts or estimated?
[10:29] Lena Park: cost in the bench report will use actual token counts captured in telemetry and Redwood's pricing matrix. if you're a dedicated or private customer you'll have different cost numbers; we'll include both hosted and dedicated projections.
[10:45] Tom Keller: do you have an example acceptance criteria doc?
[10:48] Lena Park: yes I'll send a template with suggested gates (we'll include the ones Diego suggested).
[10:55] Maya Singh: one more question — how do you handle model rollouts during the POC? we need reproducibility.
[11:02] Diego Ramos: the harness pins a model_version string; we snapshot the runtime and log the exact model artifact hash, quantization profile, and kernel selection. you'll get a reproducible report with figures and the raw telemetry.
[11:20] Rita O'Neal: logging retention and access for audit — will Redwood host the telemetry or push to our S3?
[11:27] Lena Park: options: (A) Redwood stores telemetry for the POC period behind your dedicated retention policy, (B) we push raw telemetry to your S3 bucket, or (C) you pull via secure API. we'll do whatever your security prefers.
[11:44] Samir Patel: ok. regarding success criteria — let's lock a draft: p95 <= 600ms for <=128 token realtime, cold 99th <= 1.5s, sustained throughput 180 req/s, KV cache hit >= 85% after warmup, error rate <0.5%. for batch: throughput target TBD after you see our tokens/sec baseline.
[12:12] Lena Park: sounds good as a starting point. we'll capture that as the preliminary acceptance gates and iterate.
[12:20] Diego Ramos: now, small nit — for the harness adapter, we need you to produce a function with this signature: run_vector(vector) -> {request_id, model, tokens_in, tokens_out, latency_ms, status}. if you can't, we'll supply a thin wrapper.
[12:35] Tom Keller: we'll adapt.
[12:38] Maya Singh: security requests: SSO/SAML for console access, SOC2 report, and clarification on KMS integration for private deploy.
[12:48] Lena Park: we'll attach SOC2 and KMS notes; Private will involve customer-managed KMS in the VPC option.
[12:55] Diego Ramos: lastly, about fallthrough routing — if the primary model degradation happens, do you want automatic fallback to a smaller variant? that changes the acceptance conversation.
[13:06] Samir Patel: not without notifying product; automatic fallback is ok only for degraded-but-functional cases. we'd like explicit flags.
[13:14] Lena Park: we can set rollouts to manual or canary; defaults are configurable.
[13:20] Maya Singh: perfect.
[13:25] (long pause, note-taking)
[13:40] Lena Park: ok we'll summarize next steps — Diego will own the streaming/non-streaming perf plan, I'll send the benchmark template and telemetry contract, and Tom will provide traces and scripts. security will get the SOC2 pack.
[13:55] Diego Ramos: and I'll draft the test matrix: short-turn streaming vs non-streaming, batch runs at 4 batch sizes, cache-warmup phase, spike test, and cold-start tail analysis.
[14:12] Maya Singh: small callout — we also want a regression test for hallucination/on-target nuisances. can you add a small eval pass that runs our prompts and checks for known hallucination triggers?
[14:25] Diego Ramos: yes we can add a prompt-eval set and capture quality metrics; we'll add that as optional acceptance criteria.
[14:38] Tom Keller: timeline again — adapter spec and template by Monday (Lena), customer traces by Thursday, dry-run mid-next week.
[14:48] Lena Park: noted.
[14:55] Samir Patel: any blockers in integration?
[15:00] Diego Ramos: only security signoff for live traces and a small shim on your runner if you want us to drive it. nothing major.
[15:12] Rita O'Neal: ok.
[15:15] Lena Park: great. I'll follow up with the email and links.

End of meeting — short recap and final Q&A happened off-record.
